claim: Neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (CbN) transmit cerebellar signals to premotor areas.
source: Neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (CbN) transmit cerebellar signals to premotor areas.
evidence: This is a statement of established neuroanatomical knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: The cerebellum expresses several autism-linked genes, including GABRB3.
source: The cerebellum expresses several autism-linked genes, including GABRB3, which encodes GABAA receptor β3 subunits and is among the maternal alleles deleted in Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about gene expression patterns and genetic associations with autism and Angelman syndrome.

claim: GABRB3 encodes GABAA receptor β3 subunits.
source: The cerebellum expresses several autism-linked genes, including GABRB3, which encodes GABAA receptor β3 subunits and is among the maternal alleles deleted in Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is established molecular biology knowledge about the GABRB3 gene.

claim: GABRB3 is among the maternal alleles deleted in Angelman syndrome.
source: The cerebellum expresses several autism-linked genes, including GABRB3, which encodes GABAA receptor β3 subunits and is among the maternal alleles deleted in Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of Angelman syndrome.

claim: Wild-type mice showed sex differences in synaptic excitation, inhibition, and intrinsic properties in CbN cells.
source: Wild-type mice showed sex differences in synaptic excitation, inhibition, and intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differences in mGluR1/5-dependent currents, IPSC kinetics, and spontaneous firing rates between males and females.

claim: CbN cells of wild-type males had smaller synaptically evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents relative to females.
source: Relative to females, CbN cells of males had smaller synaptically evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents, slower Purkinje-mediated IPSCs, and lower spontaneous firing rates, but rotarod performances were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 comparing tonic currents and CPCCOEt-sensitive currents between males and females.

claim: CbN cells of wild-type males had slower Purkinje-mediated IPSCs relative to females.
source: Relative to females, CbN cells of males had smaller synaptically evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents, slower Purkinje-mediated IPSCs, and lower spontaneous firing rates, but rotarod performances were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing IPSC decay time constants.

claim: CbN cells of wild-type males had lower spontaneous firing rates relative to females.
source: Relative to females, CbN cells of males had smaller synaptically evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents, slower Purkinje-mediated IPSCs, and lower spontaneous firing rates, but rotarod performances were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B comparing spontaneous firing rates between males and females.

claim: Rotarod performances were indistinguishable between wild-type males and females.
source: Relative to females, CbN cells of males had smaller synaptically evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents, slower Purkinje-mediated IPSCs, and lower spontaneous firing rates, but rotarod performances were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A comparing rotarod performance between wild-type males and females.

claim: In mutant CbN cells, IPSC kinetics were unchanged.
source: In mutant CbN cells, IPSC kinetics were unchanged, but mutant males, unlike females, showed enlarged mGluR1/5 responses and accelerated spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E comparing IPSC decay time constants between wild-type and mutant mice.

claim: Mutant males showed enlarged mGluR1/5 responses.
source: In mutant CbN cells, IPSC kinetics were unchanged, but mutant males, unlike females, showed enlarged mGluR1/5 responses and accelerated spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 comparing tonic currents and CPCCOEt-sensitive currents between wild-type and mutant males.

claim: Mutant males showed accelerated spontaneous firing.
source: In mutant CbN cells, IPSC kinetics were unchanged, but mutant males, unlike females, showed enlarged mGluR1/5 responses and accelerated spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B comparing spontaneous firing rates between wild-type and mutant males.

claim: Mutant females did not show enlarged mGluR1/5 responses.
source: In mutant CbN cells, IPSC kinetics were unchanged, but mutant males, unlike females, showed enlarged mGluR1/5 responses and accelerated spontaneous firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 showing no difference in tonic currents between wild-type and mutant females.

claim: The changes in mutant males appear compensatory.
source: These changes appear compensatory, since mutant males but not females performed indistinguishably from wild-type siblings on the rotarod task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males show electrophysiological changes but normal behavior, suggesting compensation.

claim: Mutant males performed indistinguishably from wild-type siblings on the rotarod task.
source: These changes appear compensatory, since mutant males but not females performed indistinguishably from wild-type siblings on the rotarod task.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A comparing rotarod performance between wild-type and mutant males.

claim: Mutant females did not perform indistinguishably from wild-type siblings on the rotarod task.
source: These changes appear compensatory, since mutant males but not females performed indistinguishably from wild-type siblings on the rotarod task.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A showing differences in rotarod performance between wild-type and mutant females.

claim: Sex differences in cerebellar physiology produce similar behavioral output.
source: Thus, sex differences in cerebellar physiology produce similar behavioral output, but provide distinct baselines for responses to mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that wild-type males and females show different physiology but similar rotarod performance.

claim: Sex differences in cerebellar physiology provide distinct baselines for responses to mutations.
source: Thus, sex differences in cerebellar physiology produce similar behavioral output, but provide distinct baselines for responses to mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that males and females respond differently to the Gabrb3 mutation.

claim: Many genes disrupted in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are expressed in the cerebellum.
source: Recent work has drawn attention to the fact that many genes disrupted in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are expressed in the cerebellum (Fatemi et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014), suggesting that, regardless of the etiology of the phenotypes associated with the condition, cerebellar processing may be affected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Fatemi et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: Cerebellar abnormalities are consistently found in post-mortem examinations of autistic brains.
source: Indeed, cerebellar abnormalities are consistently found in post-mortem examinations of autistic brains, which reveal decreases in size and number of Purkinje and/or CbN cells (Bauman and Kemper, 1985; Arin et al., 1991; Bailey et al., 1998; Kemper and Bauman, 1998; Whitney et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Post-mortem examinations of autistic brains reveal decreases in size and number of Purkinje and/or CbN cells.
source: Indeed, cerebellar abnormalities are consistently found in post-mortem examinations of autistic brains, which reveal decreases in size and number of Purkinje and/or CbN cells (Bauman and Kemper, 1985; Arin et al., 1991; Bailey et al., 1998; Kemper and Bauman, 1998; Whitney et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Mice with the 15q11-13 duplication show defects in cerebellar learning.
source: Mice with the 15q11-13 duplication, a model for one form of autism, show defects in cerebellar learning (Piochon et al., 2014), and mutation of Tsc1 in Purkinje cells alone can recapitulate several autism-like behaviors in mice (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Piochon et al., 2014.

claim: Mutation of Tsc1 in Purkinje cells alone can recapitulate several autism-like behaviors in mice.
source: Mice with the 15q11-13 duplication, a model for one form of autism, show defects in cerebellar learning (Piochon et al., 2014), and mutation of Tsc1 in Purkinje cells alone can recapitulate several autism-like behaviors in mice (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: Angelman syndrome patients have a microdeletion of the 15q11-13 region of the maternal chromosome.
source: These patients have a microdeletion of the 15q11-13 region of the maternal chromosome, which spans multiple genes (Knoll et al., 1989), of which UBE3A and GABRB3 have been the most extensively studied.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Knoll et al., 1989.

claim: UBE3A and GABRB3 have been the most extensively studied genes in the 15q11-13 region.
source: These patients have a microdeletion of the 15q11-13 region of the maternal chromosome, which spans multiple genes (Knoll et al., 1989), of which UBE3A and GABRB3 have been the most extensively studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the research literature on Angelman syndrome.

claim: Mice lacking maternal Ube3a recapitulate many but not all phenotypes expected for an animal model of Angelman syndrome.
source: Mice lacking maternal Ube3a recapitulate many but not all phenotypes expected for an animal model of Angelman syndrome (Jiang et al., 1998; Allensworth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jiang et al., 1998 and Allensworth et al., 2011.

claim: Adult Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice display deficits in motor learning as measured by the accelerating rotarod task.
source: Regarding cerebellar function, adult Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice display deficits in motor learning as measured by the accelerating rotarod task (DeLorey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DeLorey et al., 2011.

claim: β3 is expressed in Purkinje and granule cells in the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, β3 is expressed in Purkinje and granule cells, with low expression in the cerebellar nuclei (Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013.

claim: β3 has low expression in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: In the cerebellum, β3 is expressed in Purkinje and granule cells, with low expression in the cerebellar nuclei (Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013.

claim: β3 slows the kinetics of GABAAR currents in expression systems.
source: Since β3 slows the kinetics of GABAAR currents in expression systems (Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003), IPSC kinetics of neurons that express GABAAR β3 are predicted to be accelerated in Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice, which should disinhibit those cells and alter signaling through the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003.

claim: IPSC kinetics of neurons that express GABAAR β3 are predicted to be accelerated in Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice.
source: Since β3 slows the kinetics of GABAAR currents in expression systems (Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003), IPSC kinetics of neurons that express GABAAR β3 are predicted to be accelerated in Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice, which should disinhibit those cells and alter signaling through the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known effect of β3 on GABAAR kinetics and the expected consequence of the mutation.

claim: Accelerated IPSC kinetics in Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice should disinhibit cells and alter signaling through the cerebellum.
source: Since β3 slows the kinetics of GABAAR currents in expression systems (Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003), IPSC kinetics of neurons that express GABAAR β3 are predicted to be accelerated in Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice, which should disinhibit those cells and alter signaling through the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the expected consequence of accelerated IPSC kinetics.

claim: A sex difference in motor behavior of m-/p+ mice has been reported.
source: Because of a reported sex difference in motor behavior of m-/p+ mice (DeLorey et al., 2011), we also compared electrophysiological responses in males and females.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DeLorey et al., 2011.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation triggers an augmentation of mGluR1/5 responses in male but not female mutant mice.
source: Males and females also respond differently to the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation, which triggers an augmentation of mGluR1/5 responses and intrinsic firing rates in male but not female mutant mice, which is apparently compensatory on a motor learning task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 5 comparing mGluR1/5 responses and firing rates between wild-type and mutant mice of both sexes.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation triggers an augmentation of intrinsic firing rates in male but not female mutant mice.
source: Males and females also respond differently to the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation, which triggers an augmentation of mGluR1/5 responses and intrinsic firing rates in male but not female mutant mice, which is apparently compensatory on a motor learning task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 comparing spontaneous firing rates between wild-type and mutant mice of both sexes.

claim: The augmentation of mGluR1/5 responses and intrinsic firing rates in male mutant mice is apparently compensatory on a motor learning task.
source: Males and females also respond differently to the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation, which triggers an augmentation of mGluR1/5 responses and intrinsic firing rates in male but not female mutant mice, which is apparently compensatory on a motor learning task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males show electrophysiological changes but normal rotarod performance.

claim: Whole-cell recordings were made from large CbN cells in cerebellar slices from P17-P24 mice.
source: Whole-cell recordings were made from large CbN cells in cerebellar slices from P17-P24 mice, and voltage-clamped synaptic currents were evoked with 100-Hz, 200-ms trains of electrical stimuli to evoke Purkinje cell-mediated IPSCs (Telgkamp and Raman, 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: 100-Hz, 200-ms trains of electrical stimuli evoke Purkinje cell-mediated IPSCs.
source: Whole-cell recordings were made from large CbN cells in cerebellar slices from P17-P24 mice, and voltage-clamped synaptic currents were evoked with 100-Hz, 200-ms trains of electrical stimuli to evoke Purkinje cell-mediated IPSCs (Telgkamp and Raman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Telgkamp and Raman, 2002.

claim: In wild-type males and females, the phasic components of IPSCs largely overlaid one another.
source: In wild-type males and females, the phasic components largely overlaid one another (Figure 1A,B; repeated-measures ANOVA p=0.78).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and statistical analysis.

claim: The tonic component of synaptic current was more than 3-fold larger in wild-type males than females.
source: In contrast, the synaptic current decayed to a greater extent in females, leading to a tonic component that was more than 3-fold larger in wild-type males than females (Figure 1A,B, +/+ males n=11, +/+ females n=10, p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and statistical analysis.

claim: The sex difference in tonic synaptic current was replicated in C57BL/6 males and females.
source: This result was replicated in C57BL/6 males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), demonstrating that elements of basal synaptic transmission in the CbN of mice differ between the sexes, even in pre-pubertal animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Elements of basal synaptic transmission in the CbN of mice differ between the sexes, even in pre-pubertal animals.
source: This result was replicated in C57BL/6 males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), demonstrating that elements of basal synaptic transmission in the CbN of mice differ between the sexes, even in pre-pubertal animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of sex differences in P17-P24 mice.

claim: Mutant males had a smaller tonic component than wild-type males.
source: Consequently, cells from mutant males had a smaller tonic component than wild-type males (m-/p+ males n=11, p=0.029), but wild-type and mutant females did not differ (m-/p+ females n=11, p=0.94).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: Wild-type and mutant females did not differ in tonic component.
source: Consequently, cells from mutant males had a smaller tonic component than wild-type males (m-/p+ males n=11, p=0.029), but wild-type and mutant females did not differ (m-/p+ females n=11, p=0.94).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation leads to a change in tonic synaptic current in males but not in females.
source: Thus, the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation leads to a change in tonic synaptic current in males but not in females, eliminating the sex difference present in wild-type animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males have reduced tonic current while mutant females do not differ from wild-type.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation eliminates the sex difference in tonic synaptic current present in wild-type animals.
source: Thus, the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation leads to a change in tonic synaptic current in males but not in females, eliminating the sex difference present in wild-type animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males and females have similar tonic currents.

claim: The weighted τdecay of IPSCs was 2.3 ± 0.1 ms in wild-type males.
source: The weighted τdecay was 2.3 ± 0.1 ms in wild-type males (n=22) and 1.8 ± 0.2 ms in wild-type females (n=9, p=0.07).
evidence: This is experimental data from IPSC decay measurements.

claim: The weighted τdecay of IPSCs was 1.8 ± 0.2 ms in wild-type females.
source: The weighted τdecay was 2.3 ± 0.1 ms in wild-type males (n=22) and 1.8 ± 0.2 ms in wild-type females (n=9, p=0.07).
evidence: This is experimental data from IPSC decay measurements.

claim: Combining datasets from Gabrb3 and C57BL/6 mice demonstrated that cells from females had significantly slower IPSC decay times than males.
source: Similar values were seen in cells from C57BL/6 mice, and combining the datasets demonstrated that cells from females indeed had significantly slower IPSC decay times than males (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, males 2.4 ± 0.1, n=33; females 1.8 ± 0.2, n=21; p=0.008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: The mean IPSC decay time constants in cells from m-/p+ mice were indistinguishable from those of wild-type, for both males and females.
source: Despite the fact that GABAAR β3 expression is expected to slow the deactivation of GABAAR currents (Hinkle and MacDonald 2003), the mean time constants in cells from m-/p+ mice were indistinguishable from those of wild-type, for both males and females (Figure 1E, solid symbols; m-/p+ males 2.5 ± 0.2 ms, n=16, p=0.5 vs. +/+; m-/p+ females 1.8 ± 0.2 ms, n=6, p=1.0 vs. +/+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis.

claim: The kinetics of evoked synaptic currents in large CbN cells do not depend strongly on GABAAR β3.
source: This similarity suggests that the kinetics of evoked synaptic currents in large CbN cells do not depend strongly on GABAAR β3, possibly because Gabrb3 m-/p+ does not actually result in reduced cerebellar expression, or because the GABAAR β3 subunit is not strongly expressed in the cerebellar nuclei even in wild-type mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IPSC kinetics are unchanged in mutant mice.

claim: β3 subunit expression in the cerebellar cortex was about twice that in the cerebellar nuclei, in both males and females.
source: Indeed, β3 subunit expression was relatively low in the CbN; β3 expression in the cerebellar cortex was about twice that in the cerebellar nuclei, in both males and females (Figure 1F, males, n=2, p=0.02, females, n=2, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Loss of the maternal Gabrb3 allele significantly reduced GABAAR β3 expression to about half in both sexes in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Consistent with a gene dosage effect, loss of the maternal Gabrb3 allele significantly reduced GABAAR β3 expression to about half in both sexes (Figure 1G, males, n=3, p=0.001; females, n=3, p=0.005).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GABAAR β3 expression in the cerebellar cortex was indistinguishable in males and females in wild-type animals.
source: In wild-type animals, expression in the cerebellar cortex was indistinguishable in males and females, in both Gabrb3 sibling controls (n=3, p=0.21) and in C57BL/6 mice (n=6, p=0.37).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data comparing males and females.

claim: GABAAR β3 expression in the cerebellar nuclei was significantly reduced in mutant males and females.
source: GABAAR β3 expression in the cerebellar nuclei was also significantly reduced in mutant males and females (p≤0.001, both sexes).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data comparing wild-type and mutant mice.

claim: The lack of changes in IPSC decay times in CbN cells of Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice is more likely to result from sparse GABAAR β3 expression in wild-type mice, rather than a failure of the mutation to reduce expression.
source: Thus, the lack of changes in IPSC decay times in CbN cells of Gabrb3 m-/p+ mice is more likely to result from sparse GABAAR β3 expression in wild-type mice, rather than a failure of the mutation to reduce expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot data showing low β3 expression in CbN and reduced expression in mutants.

claim: The decay time constants of IPSCs lengthened during the train.
source: The decay time constants, however, lengthened during the train, such that the last IPSC was significantly longer than the first for wild-type males (Figure 1E, open symbols; weighted τdecay for last IPSC, +/+ males, 4.4 ± 0.7 ms, n=10, p=0.013 vs. 1st IPSC; m-/p+ males, 3.2 ± 0.8 ms, n=11, p=0.36; +/+ females, 2.3 ± 0.3 ms, n=10, p=0.21; m-/p+ females, 3.1 ± 0.8 ms, n=11, p=0.17).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E comparing first and last IPSC decay times.

claim: For wild-type males, the predicted and measured tonic currents were closely matched.
source: As shown in Figure 1H, for wild-type males, the predicted and measured currents were closely matched (solid and open black triangles), indicating that IPSC kinetics are sufficient to account for the tonic synaptic current.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H comparing predicted and measured tonic currents.

claim: IPSC kinetics are sufficient to account for the tonic synaptic current in wild-type males.
source: As shown in Figure 1H, for wild-type males, the predicted and measured currents were closely matched (solid and open black triangles), indicating that IPSC kinetics are sufficient to account for the tonic synaptic current.
evidence: This is an inference based on the close match between predicted and measured tonic currents in wild-type males.

claim: For mutant males and both female groups, the IPSC decay times predicted a tonic current that is smaller than in wild-type males but still larger than the measured values.
source: For mutant males and both female groups, however, the IPSC decay times consistently predicted a tonic current that is smaller than in wild-type males but still larger than the measured values (open vs. solid symbols), suggesting an additional factor either reducing the total outward tonic current or contributing a tonic inward current.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H comparing predicted and measured tonic currents.

claim: An additional factor is either reducing the total outward tonic current or contributing a tonic inward current in mutant males and both female groups.
source: For mutant males and both female groups, however, the IPSC decay times consistently predicted a tonic current that is smaller than in wild-type males but still larger than the measured values (open vs. solid symbols), suggesting an additional factor either reducing the total outward tonic current or contributing a tonic inward current.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between predicted and measured tonic currents.

claim: Glutamate release from mossy fibers can activate group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1/5) in CbN neurons.
source: One possibility arose from the fact that in the experiments of Figure 1, only fast excitatory transmission was blocked. Previous work, however, shows that glutamate release from mossy fibers can activate group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1/5) in CbN neurons, which in turn can increase tonic inward currents through multiple mechanisms (Zhang and Linden, 2006; Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Linden, 2006 and Zheng and Raman, 2011.

claim: Group I mGluRs can increase tonic inward currents through multiple mechanisms in CbN neurons.
source: One possibility arose from the fact that in the experiments of Figure 1, only fast excitatory transmission was blocked. Previous work, however, shows that glutamate release from mossy fibers can activate group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1/5) in CbN neurons, which in turn can increase tonic inward currents through multiple mechanisms (Zhang and Linden, 2006; Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang and Linden, 2006 and Zheng and Raman, 2011.

claim: CPCCOEt effectively blocks group I mGluRs in CbN cells.
source: We therefore tested the effect of CPCCOEt (100 µM), which effectively blocks group I mGluRs in CbN cells in a manner that is mimicked by a combination of the selective mGluR1 antagonist JNJ16259685 and mGluR5 antagonist MPEP (Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng and Raman, 2011.

claim: CPCCOEt increased the net outward tonic current in CbN cells of wild-type and mutant mice of both sexes.
source: When trains of IPSCs were evoked, CPCCOEt increased the net outward tonic current, consistent with activation of group I mGluRs in CbN cells of wild-type and mutant mice of both sexes (+/+ males n=11, females n=11; m-/p+ males n=12, females n=9, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 comparing tonic currents in control and CPCCOEt.

claim: CPCCOEt eliminated the sex difference between wild-type male and female tonic currents.
source: Importantly, CPCCOEt also eliminated the sex difference between wild-type male and female tonic currents (Figure 2A,B, p=0.93).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B and statistical analysis.

claim: The tonic currents in mutant cells were indistinguishable from those of wild-type cells in CPCCOEt.
source: Additionally, the tonic currents in mutant cells were indistinguishable from those of wild-type cells (Figure 2C,D, males, p=1.0; females, p=0.93), suggesting that the observed sex difference in wild-type synaptic currents results from a larger mGluR1/5 response in females than in males.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: The observed sex difference in wild-type synaptic currents results from a larger mGluR1/5 response in females than in males.
source: Additionally, the tonic currents in mutant cells were indistinguishable from those of wild-type cells (Figure 2C,D, males, p=1.0; females, p=0.93), suggesting that the observed sex difference in wild-type synaptic currents results from a larger mGluR1/5 response in females than in males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CPCCOEt eliminates the sex difference in tonic currents.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation increases the mGluR1/5 response in males, but not in females.
source: The difference in tonic current in control and CPCCOEt (Figure 2E) provides a measure of the differential contribution of group I mGluRs. Thus, the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation increases the mGluR1/5 response in males, but not in females.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E comparing the CPCCOEt-sensitive current between groups.

claim: CPCCOEt prolonged the time course of decay of a single IPSC for all four groups.
source: CPCCOEt, however, did consistently prolong the time course of decay of a single IPSC for all four groups (p<0.001, in CPCCOEt, +/+ males n=13, +/+ females n=6, m-/p+ males n=10, m-/p+ females n=6, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and statistical analysis.

claim: Group I mGluRs may be basally activated in a manner that shortens synaptic currents.
source: This effect on even a single stimulus suggests that group I mGluRs may be basally activated in a manner that shortens synaptic currents, e.g., by inhibition of presynaptic Ca currents (Xu-Friedman and Regehr, 2000).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that CPCCOEt prolongs IPSC decay, with a citation to a possible mechanism.

claim: Application of TBOA evoked a large standing current of a few hundred pA at -40 mV.
source: In the present experiments, however, application of TBOA had a striking effect even in the absence of synaptic stimulation: it evoked a large standing current of a few hundred pA at -40 mV, which was largely reversed by group I mGluR antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TBOA-induced standing current was largely reversed by group I mGluR antagonists.
source: In the present experiments, however, application of TBOA had a striking effect even in the absence of synaptic stimulation: it evoked a large standing current of a few hundred pA at -40 mV, which was largely reversed by group I mGluR antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TBOA-induced current was reversed by TTX.
source: The TBOA-induced current was indeed reversed by TTX (Figure 3B, C57BL/6 male mice; control -305 ± 99 pA; TBOA -570 ± 139 pA, p=0.033 vs. control; TBOA+TTX -338 ± 43 pA, p=0.2 vs. control), and the variance of the standing current was reduced.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: Spontaneously firing nearby cells continuously release glutamate.
source: The data are consistent with the idea that spontaneously firing nearby cells continuously release glutamate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the TBOA-induced current is reversed by TTX.

claim: In the presence of TBOA, the released glutamate reaches and activates group I mGluRs on CbN cells.
source: In the presence of TBOA, the released glutamate reaches and activates group I mGluRs on CbN cells, which in turn couple to other channels; at this voltage, the inward current is likely carried primarily through L-type Ca channels (Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TBOA increases mGluR1/5-dependent current, with a citation to the downstream mechanism.

claim: At -40 mV, the inward current is likely carried primarily through L-type Ca channels.
source: In the presence of TBOA, the released glutamate reaches and activates group I mGluRs on CbN cells, which in turn couple to other channels; at this voltage, the inward current is likely carried primarily through L-type Ca channels (Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng and Raman, 2011.

claim: Blocking glutamate transport revealed an increase in mGluR1/5-dependent current amplitude at -40 mV that was, on average, larger in wild-type males than in wild-type females.
source: Unlike the evoked currents measured in Figures 1 and 2, however, blocking glutamate transport revealed an increase in mGluR1/5-dependent current amplitude at -40 mV that was, on average, larger in wild-type males than in wild-type females (Figure 3A, +/+ males -297 ± 67 pA, n=9; +/+ females -184 ± 64 pA, n=9, p=0.08).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no difference in TBOA-induced current between sex-matched mutant vs. wild-type groups.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference between sex-matched mutant vs. wild-type groups (m-/p+ males -419 ± 99 pA, n=11, p=0.5 vs. +/+; m-/p+ females -184 ± 65, n=9, p=0.9 vs. +/+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing TBOA-induced currents between wild-type and mutant mice.

claim: The differences in evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents do not necessarily result from fewer receptors or diminished properties of downstream targets in wild-type males.
source: These results suggest that the differences in evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents do not necessarily result from fewer receptors or diminished properties of downstream targets in wild-type males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TBOA reveals similar or larger mGluR1/5 responses in wild-type males.

claim: The reduced response to evoked release in wild-type males may stem from the accessibility of glutamate to mGluRs when transport is intact.
source: Instead, the reduced response to evoked release in wild-type males may stem from the accessibility of glutamate to mGluRs when transport is intact, i.e., owing to differences in the efficacy of uptake or proximity of receptors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that blocking transport reveals larger mGluR1/5 responses in wild-type males.

claim: The Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation does not apparently alter the maximal mGluR1/5 response, as measured with transporter blockers, in males or females.
source: Moreover, the Gabrb3 m-/p+ mutation does not apparently alter the maximal mGluR1/5 response, as measured with transporter blockers, in males or females.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TBOA-induced currents are similar between wild-type and mutant mice.

claim: Neither mGluR1 nor mGluR5 protein levels differed significantly between wild-type males and females.
source: Indeed, neither mGluR1 nor mGluR5 protein levels differed significantly between wild-type males and females, or between wild-type males and mutant males (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: mGluR1 and mGluR5 protein levels did not differ between wild-type males and mutant males.
source: Indeed, neither mGluR1 nor mGluR5 protein levels differed significantly between wild-type males and females, or between wild-type males and mutant males (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The smaller evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents observed in wild-type males arise largely from access of glutamate to group I mGluRs.
source: In conjunction with the electrophysiological data in TBOA, these results support the idea that the smaller evoked mGluR1/5-dependent currents observed in wild-type males, relative to wild-type females or mutant males, arise largely from access of glutamate to group I mGluRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking transport reveals similar mGluR1/5 responses across groups, while receptor expression is similar.

claim: The initial peak EPSC was decreased in TBOA by about 50% in all groups but wild-type females.
source: The initial peak EPSC was decreased in TBOA by about 50% in all groups but wild-type females (+/+ males p=0.008, n=7; m-/p+ males p=0.047, n=7; +/+ females p=0.65, n=6; m-/p+ females p=0.006, n=8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and statistical analysis.

claim: The EPSC amplitude was not further changed by application of group I mGluR antagonists.
source: The EPSC amplitude was not further changed by application of group I mGluR antagonists, however (Figure 4A,B, vs. TBOA, +/+ males p=0.18, m-/p+ males p=0.97, +/+ females p=0.27, m-/p+ females p=0.66), suggesting that glutamate accumulation induced by TBOA may decrease EPSC amplitude by acting at other receptors, e.g., group II/III mGluRs, or by directly desensitizing AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B and statistical analysis.

claim: Glutamate accumulation induced by TBOA may decrease EPSC amplitude by acting at other receptors or by directly desensitizing AMPA receptors.
source: The EPSC amplitude was not further changed by application of group I mGluR antagonists, however (Figure 4A,B, vs. TBOA, +/+ males p=0.18, m-/p+ males p=0.97, +/+ females p=0.27, m-/p+ females p=0.66), suggesting that glutamate accumulation induced by TBOA may decrease EPSC amplitude by acting at other receptors, e.g., group II/III mGluRs, or by directly desensitizing AMPA receptors.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that mGluR1/5 antagonists do not reverse the TBOA-induced decrease in EPSC amplitude.

claim: In wild-type males, TBOA reduced synaptic depression.
source: In wild-type males, however, TBOA reduced synaptic depression (+/+ males, control 38 ± 7%, TBOA 52 ± 7%, p=0.012), and, unlike the change in initial EPSC amplitude, the effect of TBOA on synaptic depression was blocked by group I mGluR antagonists (+/+ males with antagonist 42 ± 6%, p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of TBOA on synaptic depression in wild-type males was blocked by group I mGluR antagonists.
source: In wild-type males, however, TBOA reduced synaptic depression (+/+ males, control 38 ± 7%, TBOA 52 ± 7%, p=0.012), and, unlike the change in initial EPSC amplitude, the effect of TBOA on synaptic depression was blocked by group I mGluR antagonists (+/+ males with antagonist 42 ± 6%, p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and statistical analysis.

claim: The lack of detectable evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in wild-type males depends on intact glutamate transport.
source: This observation lends support to the idea that the lack of detectable evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in wild-type males depends on intact glutamate transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking transport reveals mGluR1/5-dependent effects in wild-type males.

claim: In both female groups, TBOA had no detectable effect on synaptic depression.
source: In contrast, in both female groups, TBOA had no detectable effect on synaptic depression (+/+ females p=0.81, m-/p+ p=0.22).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and statistical analysis.

claim: CbN cells fired more slowly in wild-type males than in females.
source: Indeed, CbN cells fired more slowly in wild-type males (65 ± 7 spikes/s, n=14) than in females (98 ± 9 spikes/s, n=16; p=0.02), again reflecting a sex difference in basic CbN cell properties (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B and statistical analysis.

claim: CbN cells from mutant males tended to fire somewhat faster than from wild-type males.
source: CbN cells from mutant males tended to fire somewhat faster than from wild-type males (92 ± 9 spikes/s, n=11, p=0.08), whereas cells from mutant females had the same firing rates as those from wild-type females (96 ± 10 spikes/s, n=20, p=0.9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing spontaneous firing rates between wild-type and mutant males.

claim: Cells from mutant females had the same firing rates as those from wild-type females.
source: CbN cells from mutant males tended to fire somewhat faster than from wild-type males (92 ± 9 spikes/s, n=11, p=0.08), whereas cells from mutant females had the same firing rates as those from wild-type females (96 ± 10 spikes/s, n=20, p=0.9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing spontaneous firing rates between wild-type and mutant females.

claim: Action potential half-widths were indistinguishable among all four groups.
source: Action potential half-widths, however, were indistinguishable among all four groups (Figure 5B, p=0.3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and statistical analysis.

claim: Holding currents at -40 mV were not different across the four groups of mice.
source: The experiments of Figure 3, however, demonstrated that holding currents at -40 mV were not different across the four groups of mice (+/+ males -565 ± 40 pA; m-/p+ males -491 ± 59 pA; +/+ females -406 ± 83 pA; m-/p+ females -424 ± 49 pA, p=0.26).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage clamp recordings.

claim: The slower firing rates in wild-type males are more likely to reflect differences in intrinsic currents.
source: It therefore seems unlikely that the slower firing rates in wild-type males arose from mGluR1/5 activation, and instead are more likely to reflect differences in intrinsic currents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that holding currents are similar across groups.

claim: After periods of spike suppression, CbN neurons increase their firing above their intrinsic rates for a few hundred milliseconds.
source: Specifically, after periods of spike suppression either by hyperpolarization or by trains of IPSCs, CbN neurons have been shown to increase their firing above their intrinsic rates for a few hundred milliseconds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CbN neuron physiology.

claim: Prolonged rebound firing depends partly on recovery of intrinsic conductances.
source: This phenomenon of 'prolonged rebound firing' depends partly on recovery of intrinsic conductances (Aman and Raman, 2007; Sangrey and Jaeger, 2010; Tadayonnejad et al., 2010) and partly on mGluR1/5 potentiation of L-type Ca currents (Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prolonged rebound firing depends partly on mGluR1/5 potentiation of L-type Ca currents.
source: This phenomenon of 'prolonged rebound firing' depends partly on recovery of intrinsic conductances (Aman and Raman, 2007; Sangrey and Jaeger, 2010; Tadayonnejad et al., 2010) and partly on mGluR1/5 potentiation of L-type Ca currents (Zheng and Raman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng and Raman, 2011.

claim: In all cells, firing rates for the 300 ms just after the stimulus were faster than firing rates during the 500 ms just before the stimulus.
source: In all cells, firing rates for the 300 ms just after the stimulus were faster than firing rates during the 500 ms just before the stimulus (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The firing rate acceleration in CbN cells was greater in m-/p+ than wild-type males.
source: Consistent with an upregulation of mGluR1/5 responses, the firing rate acceleration in CbN cells was greater in m-/p+ than wild-type males.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D comparing prolonged rebound firing between wild-type and mutant males.

claim: In wild-type males, only 7 ± 14% of the firing rate increase after inhibition can be attributed to group I mGluRs.
source: In contrast, in CbN cells from wild-type males, only 7 ± 14% of the firing rate increase after inhibition can be attributed to group I mGluRs, while for cells from m-/p+ males, 53 ± 13% is CPCCOEt-dependent (p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and statistical analysis.

claim: For cells from m-/p+ males, 53 ± 13% of the firing rate increase after inhibition is CPCCOEt-dependent.
source: In contrast, in CbN cells from wild-type males, only 7 ± 14% of the firing rate increase after inhibition can be attributed to group I mGluRs, while for cells from m-/p+ males, 53 ± 13% is CPCCOEt-dependent (p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and statistical analysis.

claim: The upregulation of the mGluR1/5 response in mutant males generates a larger potentiation of L-type currents.
source: The larger CPCCOEt effect in mutant males is consistent with the idea that the upregulation of the mGluR1/5 response indeed generates a larger potentiation of L-type currents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males show greater CPCCOEt-sensitive prolonged rebound firing.

claim: Wild-type males and females performed the rotarod task equivalently.
source: Notably, despite the differences in basal physiology, wild-type males and females performed the task equivalently (p=0.21).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: Wild-type brains of different sexes may use different synaptic and cellular mechanisms to achieve a common behavioral output.
source: This observation demonstrates that the larger mGluR1/5 responses and faster firing rates seen in CbN cells of females do not directly translate to enhanced rotarod performance per se, instead illustrating that wild-type brains of different sexes may use different synaptic and cellular mechanisms to achieve a common behavioral output (De Vries, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that males and females show different physiology but similar behavior, with a citation to a relevant concept.

claim: Mutant males performed indistinguishably from wild-type male siblings on the rotarod.
source: Comparing the responses of mutant mice to sex-matched controls showed that mutant males performed indistinguishably from wild-type male siblings: both groups remained on the rotarod for a similar duration on Day 1 (+/+ 102 ± 14; m-/p+ 101 ± 10 s, p=0.9, for all groups n=8) and improved their performance by Day 7 (+/+ 142 ± 11; m-/p+ 133 ± 12 s; change over training assessed by repeated measures ANOVA, +/+, p=0.02; m-/p+, p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: Female m-/p+ mice tended to remain on the rod for a longer time on Day 1 than wild-type siblings.
source: In contrast, female m-/p+ mice tended to remain on the rod for a longer time on Day 1 than wild-type siblings (+/+ 78 ± 6; m-/p+ 135 ± 11 s, p=0.001), and their performance remained relatively constant over 7 days, unlike wild-type females, whose latency to fall increased (Day 7 latency, +/+ 130 ± 13; m-/p+ 116 ± 13 s; repeated measures ANOVA, +/+, p<0.00; m-/p+, p=0.3, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: The performance of female m-/p+ mice remained relatively constant over 7 days.
source: In contrast, female m-/p+ mice tended to remain on the rod for a longer time on Day 1 than wild-type siblings (+/+ 78 ± 6; m-/p+ 135 ± 11 s, p=0.001), and their performance remained relatively constant over 7 days, unlike wild-type females, whose latency to fall increased (Day 7 latency, +/+ 130 ± 13; m-/p+ 116 ± 13 s; repeated measures ANOVA, +/+, p<0.00; m-/p+, p=0.3, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A and statistical analysis.

claim: The lack of increase in fall latency over training in female mutants indicates an enhanced initial ability coupled with either a failure to improve, or a saturation of performance that precludes further improvement.
source: Given the long but replicable latency to fall on Day 1 of female mutants, the lack of increase in fall latency over training indicates an enhanced initial ability coupled with either a failure to improve, or a saturation of performance that precludes further improvement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female mutants show high initial performance but no improvement.

claim: A similarly enhanced performance by naïve mice has been reported previously for other mutations.
source: A similarly enhanced performance by naïve mice has been reported previously for other mutations (Vitali and Clarke, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vitali and Clarke, 2004.

claim: Purkinje-specific mutant males did not differ from wild-type males on the rotarod.
source: Like the global mutants, Purkinje-specific mutant males did not differ from wild-type males (Δ latency for Pkj +/+ males 12 ± 4 s, n=10; Pkj m-/p+ males 8 ± 3 s, n=11; p=0.40), while Purkinje-specific mutant females had a significantly reduced Δ latency when compared to wild-type females (Δ latency Pkj +/+ females 16 ± 4 s, n=10; Pkj m-/p+ females -1.4 ± 4 s, n=9; p=0.004, Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: Purkinje-specific mutant females had a significantly reduced Δ latency when compared to wild-type females.
source: Like the global mutants, Purkinje-specific mutant males did not differ from wild-type males (Δ latency for Pkj +/+ males 12 ± 4 s, n=10; Pkj m-/p+ males 8 ± 3 s, n=11; p=0.40), while Purkinje-specific mutant females had a significantly reduced Δ latency when compared to wild-type females (Δ latency Pkj +/+ females 16 ± 4 s, n=10; Pkj m-/p+ females -1.4 ± 4 s, n=9; p=0.004, Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: Disrupting Gabrb3 expression in Purkinje cells alone is sufficient to cause the behavioral alterations observed in mutant females, but not males.
source: Thus, disrupting Gabrb3 expression in Purkinje cells alone is sufficient to cause the behavioral alterations observed in mutant females, but not males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Purkinje-specific mutants show similar behavioral phenotypes to global mutants.

claim: A basal sex difference in tonic outward current was evident in Purkinje-specific Gabrb3 mice.
source: As before, a basal sex difference was evident, as the tonic outward current produced by a 100-Hz train stimuli was higher in wild-type males than in wild-type females (Figure 7A-7D, tonic current for last IPSC, Pkj +/+ males 7.3 ± 2.5%, n=8; Pkj +/+ females 1.5 ± 2.1%, n=9; repeated measures ANOVA p=0.06).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-D and statistical analysis.

claim: Purkinje-specific mutant males had less tonic current than wild-type males.
source: In addition, the Purkinje-specific mutant males had less tonic current than wild-type males (Pkj m-/p+ males 0.04 ± 1.5%, n=8, p=0.02 vs. Pkj +/+), consistent with an upregulation of mGluR1/5-dependent current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and statistical analysis.

claim: Wild-type and mutant Purkinje-specific females had similar levels of tonic current.
source: In contrast, wild-type and mutant females had similar levels of tonic current (Pkj m-/p+ females -2.8 ± 2.0%, n=7, p=0.14 vs. Pkj +/+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and statistical analysis.

claim: IPSCs in CbN cells on the 129S background were slower in wild-type males than in wild-type females.
source: In addition, measurements of IPSC decay kinetics were similar in the Purkinje-specific and global mutants. IPSCs in CbN cells on the 129S background were again slower in wild-type males than in wild-type females (Figure 7E, Pkj +/+ males τdecay = 3.1 ± 0.6 ms, n=6; Pkj +/+ females 1.8 ± 0.2 ms, n=7, p=0.02), and neither mutant males nor mutant females differed from their sex-matched controls (Pkj m-/p+ males 2.2 ± 0.6 ms, n=3, p=0.19 vs. Pkj +/+; Pkj m-/p+ females 1.5 ± 0.2 ms, n=5, p=0.61 vs. Pkj +/+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and statistical analysis.

claim: Neither Purkinje-specific mutant males nor mutant females differed from their sex-matched controls in IPSC decay kinetics.
source: In addition, measurements of IPSC decay kinetics were similar in the Purkinje-specific and global mutants. IPSCs in CbN cells on the 129S background were again slower in wild-type males than in wild-type females (Figure 7E, Pkj +/+ males τdecay = 3.1 ± 0.6 ms, n=6; Pkj +/+ females 1.8 ± 0.2 ms, n=7, p=0.02), and neither mutant males nor mutant females differed from their sex-matched controls (Pkj m-/p+ males 2.2 ± 0.6 ms, n=3, p=0.19 vs. Pkj +/+; Pkj m-/p+ females 1.5 ± 0.2 ms, n=5, p=0.61 vs. Pkj +/+).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and statistical analysis.

claim: The Purkinje-specific mutation reproduces the enhanced tonic inward current in mutant males but not females.
source: Together, the data illustrate that the Purkinje-specific mutation reproduces the enhanced tonic inward current in mutant males but not females, as well as the cerebellar behavioral alteration in mutant females but not males.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Purkinje-specific mutants show similar electrophysiological and behavioral phenotypes to global mutants.

claim: The upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in CbN cells of mutant males arises indirectly from the reduced GABAAR β3 subunit in the cerebellar cortex.
source: These results support the hypothesis that the upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in CbN cells of mutant males arises indirectly from the reduced GABAAR β3 subunit in the cerebellar cortex, and strongly suggest that this upregulation serves a compensatory role in cerebellar motor learning tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Purkinje-specific mutation is sufficient to produce the electrophysiological changes.

claim: The upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in CbN cells of mutant males serves a compensatory role in cerebellar motor learning tasks.
source: These results support the hypothesis that the upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent current in CbN cells of mutant males arises indirectly from the reduced GABAAR β3 subunit in the cerebellar cortex, and strongly suggest that this upregulation serves a compensatory role in cerebellar motor learning tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males show electrophysiological changes but normal behavior.

claim: The reduced expression of GABAAR β3 leads to an upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent inward currents in large premotor cells of the CbN in male but not female mutant mice.
source: The reduced expression of GABAAR β3 leads to an upregulation of evoked mGluR1/5-dependent inward currents in large premotor cells of the CbN in male but not female mutant mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The GABAAR β3 subunit is expected to prolong IPSCs in cells that express it.
source: Since the GABAAR β3 subunit is expected to prolong IPSCs (Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003) in cells that express it, i.e., Purkinje and cerebellar granule cells (Figure 1F; Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013), reduced GABAAR β3 expression in m-/p+ mice is predicted to disinhibit granule and Purkinje cells during behaviors that normally engage cerebellar cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known effect of β3 on IPSC kinetics and the expression pattern of β3.

claim: Reduced GABAAR β3 expression in m-/p+ mice is predicted to disinhibit granule and Purkinje cells during behaviors that normally engage cerebellar cortical interneurons.
source: Since the GABAAR β3 subunit is expected to prolong IPSCs (Hinkle and Macdonald, 2003) in cells that express it, i.e., Purkinje and cerebellar granule cells (Figure 1F; Laurie et al., 1992; Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Hörtnagl et al., 2013), reduced GABAAR β3 expression in m-/p+ mice is predicted to disinhibit granule and Purkinje cells during behaviors that normally engage cerebellar cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the expected consequence of reduced β3 expression.

claim: The simplest mode of counterbalancing the resulting elevation of inhibition to CbN cells would be by increasing the net excitatory drive and/or raising intrinsic excitability.
source: The simplest mode of counterbalancing the resulting elevation of inhibition to CbN cells would be by increasing the net excitatory drive and/or raising intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of compensation.

claim: Evidence for both increased excitatory drive and raised intrinsic excitability were observed in male m-/p+ mice.
source: Indeed, evidence for both changes were observed in male m-/p+ mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data on mGluR1/5 responses and firing rates.

claim: The larger mGluR1/5-dependent currents evoked by stimulation of excitatory afferents serve to counteract much of the tonic outward current elicited by concurrent stimulation of inhibitory afferents.
source: The larger mGluR1/5-dependent currents evoked by stimulation of excitatory afferents serve to counteract much of the tonic outward current elicited by concurrent stimulation of inhibitory afferents, and the increased activation of group I mGluRs is sufficient to raise excitability, as evident by the facilitation of prolonged rebound firing relative to wild-type cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mGluR1/5 currents are inward and oppose outward inhibitory currents.

claim: The increased activation of group I mGluRs is sufficient to raise excitability, as evident by the facilitation of prolonged rebound firing relative to wild-type cells.
source: The larger mGluR1/5-dependent currents evoked by stimulation of excitatory afferents serve to counteract much of the tonic outward current elicited by concurrent stimulation of inhibitory afferents, and the increased activation of group I mGluRs is sufficient to raise excitability, as evident by the facilitation of prolonged rebound firing relative to wild-type cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males show enhanced prolonged rebound firing.

claim: The increase in spontaneous firing rates in mutant males suggests that one or more intrinsic ion channels may also be modulated by the mutation.
source: In addition, the increase in spontaneous firing rates in mutant males, which occurs without a measurable increase in holding current when cells are voltage-clamped, suggests that one or more intrinsic ion channels may also be modulated by the mutation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that firing rates increase without changes in holding current.

claim: The observed increase in mGluR1/5-dependent current and intrinsic excitability in male Gabrb3 m-/p+ CbN cells is well suited to compensate for the predicted increase in inhibitory drive.
source: Independently of mechanism, the observed increase in mGluR1/5-dependent current and intrinsic excitability in male Gabrb3 m-/p+ CbN cells is well suited to compensate for the predicted increase in inhibitory drive (Figure 8, top).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the changes in mutant males would counteract increased inhibition.

claim: The results from the rotarod experiments suggest that this compensation successfully prevents mutant males from displaying altered motor behavior.
source: Indeed, the results from the rotarod experiments suggest that this compensation successfully prevents mutant males from displaying altered motor behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant males perform normally on the rotarod.

claim: CbN cells from wild-type females already have elevated spontaneous firing rates and relatively large evoked mGluR1/5 responses.
source: Males and females respond differently to the m-/p+ mutation; although GABAAR β3 protein levels are reduced in m-/p+ females, CbN cells from wild-type females already have elevated spontaneous firing rates and relatively large evoked mGluR1/5 responses, and no further changes in these parameters are seen with the mutation (Figure 8, bottom).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data comparing males and females.

claim: No further changes in spontaneous firing rates and mGluR1/5 responses are seen with the mutation in females.
source: Males and females respond differently to the m-/p+ mutation; although GABAAR β3 protein levels are reduced in m-/p+ females, CbN cells from wild-type females already have elevated spontaneous firing rates and relatively large evoked mGluR1/5 responses, and no further changes in these parameters are seen with the mutation (Figure 8, bottom).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data comparing wild-type and mutant females.

claim: The difference in rotarod behavior between wild-type and mutant weanling females suggests that the absence of an indirect response has behavioral consequences.
source: The difference in rotarod behavior between wild-type and mutant weanling females in the global and Purkinje-specific Gabrb3 mice suggests that this absence of an indirect response has behavioral consequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant females show altered rotarod behavior.

claim: Naïve mutant females show prolonged latency to fall on Day 1 of the rotarod task.
source: The disruption in rotarod performance in mutant females is unusual: naïve mutant females show prolonged latency to fall on Day 1, and fall latency is not prolonged by subsequent training.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fall latency is not prolonged by subsequent training in mutant females.
source: The disruption in rotarod performance in mutant females is unusual: naïve mutant females show prolonged latency to fall on Day 1, and fall latency is not prolonged by subsequent training.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hyperactivity has been observed in homozygous mutant Gabrb3 mice.
source: Hyperactivity has been observed in homozygous mutant Gabrb3 mice (DeLorey et al., 1998; Liljelund et al., 2005), but not in m-/p+ (Liljelund et al., 2005) or mixed paternal/maternal heterozygotes (DeLorey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DeLorey et al., 1998 and Liljelund et al., 2005.

claim: Hyperactivity has not been observed in m-/p+ mice.
source: Hyperactivity has been observed in homozygous mutant Gabrb3 mice (DeLorey et al., 1998; Liljelund et al., 2005), but not in m-/p+ (Liljelund et al., 2005) or mixed paternal/maternal heterozygotes (DeLorey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liljelund et al., 2005.

claim: m-/p+ females may be more hyperactive than m-/p+ males.
source: Neither of these studies separated mice by sex, however, leaving open the possibility that m-/p+ females are more hyperactive than m-/p+ males, which may contribute to their prolonged fall latency early in the task without improvement over the training period.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that previous studies did not separate by sex.

claim: The change in evoked mGluR1/5 responses upon loss of GABAAR β3 illustrates the extensive plasticity of the cerebellar circuit.
source: The change in evoked mGluR1/5 responses upon loss of GABAAR β3 illustrates the extensive plasticity of the cerebellar circuit, which often appears homeostatic in response to physiological perturbations and can be at least partly compensatory in response to genetic disruptions (Zheng and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the cerebellum shows compensatory changes in response to the mutation, with a citation to a relevant concept.

claim: In the pcd and lurcher mutations, loss of inhibitory input to CbN neurons from degeneration of Purkinje cells triggers structural and physiological changes that increase the efficacy of the residual inhibition.
source: For example, in the pcd and lurcher mutations, loss of inhibitory input to CbN neurons from degeneration of Purkinje cells triggers structural and physiological changes that increase the efficacy of the residual inhibition (Garin et al., 2002; Sultan et al., 2002; Linneman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garin et al., 2002; Sultan et al., 2002; Linneman et al., 2004.

claim: The sex differences in CbN cell physiology seem likely to arise from a sex difference in neuronal properties rather than from modulation by circulating gonadal hormones.
source: Although the etiology of these differences has yet to be fully examined, they seem likely to arise from a sex difference in neuronal properties rather than from modulation by circulating gonadal hormones, since they are present in pre-pubertal mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sex differences are present in pre-pubertal mice.

claim: Calbindin expression in Purkinje neurons is higher in weanling females than males.
source: For instance, calbindin expression in Purkinje neurons is higher in weanling females than males; this difference is determined by sex chromosome complement, regardless of gonadal sex (Abel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Abel et al., 2011.

claim: PGE2 can activate aromatase, and the resulting estradiol synthesis within the cerebellum leads to reduced Purkinje cell dendritic arborization in rat pups.
source: Another example of pre-pubertal cerebellar sex differences comes from rat pups, in which the inflammation-associated prostaglandin PGE2 can activate aromatase, and the resulting estradiol synthesis within the cerebellum leads to reduced Purkinje cell dendritic arborization (Sakamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakamoto et al., 2001.

claim: A decrease in Purkinje cell capacitance can be mimicked by exogenous estradiol in males but not females, even in juvenile rodent brains.
source: A decrease in Purkinje cell capacitance, as a proxy for arborization, can be mimicked by exogenous estradiol in males but not females, even in juvenile rodent brains (Dean et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dean et al., 2012.

claim: The reeler and staggerer mutations have earlier and/or more extreme effects in heterozygous males than females.
source: Precedent also exists for the idea that genetic mutations in the cerebellum are differentially manifested between the sexes; the reeler and staggerer mutations, which both lead to Purkinje cell degeneration, have earlier and/or more extreme effects in heterozygous males than females, with differences evident in animals as young as one month old (Hadj-Sahraoui et al., 1996; Doulazmi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hadj-Sahraoui et al., 1996 and Doulazmi et al., 1999.

claim: Potentiation of L-type Ca channels by group I mGluRs can accelerate prolonged rebound firing.
source: Metabotropic glutamate receptors and their downstream targets have varied effects in the cerebellar nuclei, such that changes in mGluR1/5-dependent current may alter cerebellar output. evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng and Raman, 2011.
